candidate.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — drug interaction risk, laboratory monitoring, and client education
candidate.educational_objective: Identify potassium-containing salt substitutes as a hyperkalemia risk during spironolactone therapy and reinforce appropriate serum-potassium monitoring.

options.A: The combination may cause hypokalemia because spironolactone increases urinary potassium loss.
options.B: The combination mainly increases calcium retention and can produce clinically important hypercalcemia.
options.C: The salt substitute is acceptable without extra monitoring because dietary potassium has little effect during therapy.
options.D: Potassium chloride can increase the risk of spironolactone-associated hyperkalemia; the client should avoid unsupervised potassium products and have serum potassium monitored as prescribed.

candidate.rationale: Spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia. Current labeling states that the risk is increased by potassium supplementation and potassium-containing salt substitutes and directs serum-potassium monitoring within 1 week of initiation or titration and regularly thereafter. A potassium-chloride salt substitute therefore raises a clinically important hyperkalemia concern rather than causing potassium loss or a calcium-retention problem.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Section 5.1 states that spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia; risk is increased by potassium supplementation and potassium-containing salt substitutes; serum potassium should be monitored within 1 week of initiation or titration and regularly thereafter.
candidate.source_locator: §5.1 Hyperkalemia; see also §7.1 Drugs and Supplements Increasing Serum Potassium.
candidate.source_organization: DailyMed, U.S. National Library of Medicine
candidate.stem: A client taking spironolactone begins using a salt substitute whose main ingredient is potassium chloride. Which nursing concern is most important?
